title: Tokenisation
blurb: How text gets chopped into pieces before a model can read it.

slides.title: Models don’t read words. They read tokens.
body: Before a language model sees your message, a tokeniser splits it into small chunks called tokens.
A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a word with its leading space, or a single punctuation mark.

visual.caption: One sentence split into seven tokens. Illustrative split — · marks a space.

slides.title: Every token is really a number
body: Each token maps to an ID in the model’s vocabulary — a fixed list of tens or hundreds of thousands of pieces.
The model only ever works with these numbers. Turning numbers back into text happens at the very end.

visual.caption: Token IDs shown here are made up for illustration — each model has its own vocabulary.

slides.title: Try it yourself
body: Type anything to get a feel for how text breaks apart.
Common words usually stay whole. Rare words, names, numbers and typos tend to split into more pieces.

visual.caption: Simplified demo. Real tokenisers learn their splits from huge amounts of text, so exact results differ.

slides.title: Why tokens matter
body: Limits and pricing are counted in tokens, not words. English averages a little under one token per word; many other languages need more.
Tokens also explain some odd slip-ups: ask a model to count the r’s in “strawberry” and it’s looking at chunks, not letters.

visual.caption: Rules of thumb for English text — actual counts vary by model and language.

quiz.question: What is a token?
options: A chunk of text — a word, part of a word or punctuation
A single letter of the alphabet
A password the model uses to log in
quiz.explanation: Tokens are chunks of text. Common words are often one token; longer or rarer words get split into several.

quiz.question: Why might a model miscount the r’s in “strawberry”?
options: It sees chunks of the word, not individual letters
It has never seen the word before
Counting is switched off by default
The word is too long to fit in memory
quiz.explanation: The model receives a few multi-letter tokens rather than ten separate letters, so letter-level tasks are surprisingly hard.

quiz.question: Roughly how many English words fit in 1,000 tokens?
quiz.explanation: A common rule of thumb is that a token is about ¾ of an English word, so 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words.
